questions.question: King Asoka of the Mauryan Empire was a follower of ___________ .
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Buddhism.
  • Ashoka converted to Buddhism following the immense bloodshed of the Kalinga War.
  • He dedicated the rest of his life to Dhamma-vijaya (victory through righteousness).
  • He sent his son Mahendra and daughter Sanghamitra to Sri Lanka to spread Buddhism.

questions.question: In south India, the ___________ was a village assembly found in areas where the landowners were not brahmins.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Ur.
  • In South Indian administration (Chola/Pallava periods):
    • Sabha: Assembly of Brahmin landowners.
    • Ur: Assembly of non-Brahmin landowners.
    • Nagaram: Organization of merchants.

questions.question: The term ‘Dhamma’ is the Prakrit word that is associated with which of the following rulers of ancient India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Ashoka.
  • Dhamma is the Prakrit form of the Sanskrit word Dharma.
  • Ashoka used inscriptions to spread the principles of Dhamma.
  • He appointed officials called Dhamma Mahamattas to spread these teachings.

questions.question: The social reformer Raja Ram Mohan Roy is associated with which socio-religious reform movement in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Brahmo Samaj.
  • (Repetition) Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj.
  • The movement rejected idol worship and polytheism.
  • It emphasized human dignity and criticized social evils like caste and Sati.

questions.question: Who was the founder of the Shunga Dynasty in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Pushyamitra.
  • Pushyamitra Shunga founded the Shunga Dynasty in 185 BC.
  • He was a Brahmin general who overthrew the last Mauryan king.
  • The capital of the Shungas was Pataliputra (and later Vidisha).

questions.question: The Bardoli Satyagraha took place in which year?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 1928.
  • The Bardoli Satyagraha was a movement of farmers against the hike in land revenue.
  • It was successfully led by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.
  • It was here that the women of Bardoli gave him the title 'Sardar'.

questions.question: Who renounced his knighthood on learning the Jallianwala Bagh massacre?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Rabindranath Tagore.
  • Rabindranath Tagore renounced his Knighthood in 1919.
  • This was a direct protest against the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre.
  • He wrote a famous letter to the Viceroy stating that "the time has come when badges of honour make our shame glaring."

questions.question: The Harappans probably got copper from present-day of _________ .
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Rajasthan.
  • The Harappans obtained copper from the Khetri mines in Rajasthan.
  • They also got tin from present-day Afghanistan/Iran and gold from Karnataka.
  • Copper was mixed with tin to produce Bronze.

questions.question: The script used by the Sunga was a variant of Brahmi, and was used to write the __________ language.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Sanskrit.
  • The Shunga period is noted for the revival of Sanskrit and Brahmanical traditions.
  • Patanjali, the author of Mahabhashya, was a contemporary of Pushyamitra Shunga.
  • The script was Shunga Brahmi, a transition towards the Gupta script.

questions.question: Who among the following addressed World Parliament of Religions at Chicago in 1893?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Swami Vivekananda.
  • Swami Vivekananda delivered a historic speech at the World Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893.
  • He introduced the philosophies of Vedanta and Yoga to the Western world.
  • His birthday (January 12) is celebrated as National Youth Day in India.

questions.question: Who among the following is the wife of Chandragupta I.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Kumaradevi.
  • Kumaradevi was a Lichchhavi princess and the wife of the Gupta king Chandragupta I.
  • This marriage alliance enhanced the prestige and power of the Guptas.
  • Chandragupta I issued special gold coins featuring both him and Kumaradevi.

questions.question: On 8 April, 1929, Bhagat Singh and B.K. Dutt threw a bomb in the __________ The aim of the event as their leaflet explained, was not to kill but “to make the deaf hear”,
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Central Legislative Assembly.
  • Bhagat Singh and B.K. Dutt threw smoke bombs into the Central Legislative Assembly in Delhi.
  • They were protesting against the Public Safety Bill and the Trade Dispute Bill.
  • They did not intend to kill, but to 'make the deaf hear' their struggle for freedom.

questions.question: Varahamihira's work Panchasiddhantika deals with ________ astronomical systems.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Five.
  • The Panchasiddhantika is a treatise on mathematical astronomy by Varahamihira.
  • It summarizes five earlier astronomical systems (Siddhantas): Surya, Romaka, Paulisa, Vasishtha, and Paitamaha.
  • Varahamihira was a famous scientist in the court of Vikramaditya.

questions.question: In which year was the first War of Independence taken place in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 1857.
  • The First War of Independence (or Great Revolt) broke out in 1857.
  • It began as a sepoy mutiny in Meerut.
  • Prominent leaders included Rani Lakshmibai, Nana Saheb, and Tantia Tope.

questions.question: Into how many ages is the prehistoric times in terms of technology divided?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Three.
  • Prehistory is traditionally divided into three stages: Paleolithic (Old Stone Age), Mesolithic (Middle Stone Age), and Neolithic (New Stone Age).
  • The broader classification is the Three-age system: Stone Age, Bronze Age, and Iron Age.

questions.question: _________ was the founder of the Widow Remarriage Association (1861)
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Mahadev Govind Ranade.
  • Mahadev Govind Ranade (M.G. Ranade) founded the Widow Remarriage Association in 1861.
  • He was a key figure in the Prarthana Samaj and a founding member of the INC.
  • He is known as the 'Mentor of Gokhale'.

questions.question: The nineteenth century saw the golden age of ________ under the patronage of Wajid Ali Shah.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Kathak.
  • The classical dance form Kathak flourished under the patronage of the last Nawab of Awadh, Wajid Ali Shah.
  • He himself was a trained dancer and musician (pen name Akhtarpiya).
  • Under him, the Lucknow Gharana of Kathak reached its peak.

questions.question: James Augustus Hickey is also known as father of __________ .
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Indian Journalism.
  • James Augustus Hickey is known as the Father of Indian Journalism.
  • He started India's first newspaper, 'The Bengal Gazette' (also known as Hickey's Gazette) in 1780.
  • It was a weekly paper published in English from Calcutta.

questions.question: Complete the sentence. "Most of Ashoka’s inscriptions __________ .”
questions.option_1: Were in Sanskrit and were written in the Brahmi script
questions.option_2: Were in Prakrit and were written in the Brahmi script
questions.option_3: were in Prakrit and were written in the Devnagri script
questions.option_4: Were in Brahmi and were written in the Prakrit script
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Were in Prakrit and were written in the Brahmi script.
  • (Duplicate context) Most of Ashoka’s inscriptions were in Prakrit and written in the Brahmi script.
  • Brahmi is the ancestor of most modern Indian scripts like Devanagari.
  • James Prinsep was the first to decipher Brahmi in 1837.

questions.question: Proposed by Lord Lytton, then viceroy of India (governed 1876-80), the act was intended to prevent the vernacular press from expressing criticism of British policies—notably, the opposition that had grown with the outset of the Second ________ (1878-80).
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Anglo-Afghan War.
  • The Vernacular Press Act (1878) was passed during the Second Anglo-Afghan War.
  • Lord Lytton wanted to suppress the criticism of his imperialistic war policies by local newspapers.
  • The Amrita Bazar Patrika famously turned into an English paper overnight to escape this act.

questions.question: The Palaeolithic period extends from 2 million years ago to about 12,000 years ago. This long stretch of time is divided into the Lower, Middle and Upper Palaeolithic. This long span of time covers ________ percent of human history.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 99.
  • The Palaeolithic period (Old Stone Age) accounts for 99% of human history.
  • It covers the time from the first use of stone tools to the beginning of the Holocene epoch.
  • It is divided into Lower, Middle, and Upper based on tool technology.

questions.question: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 granted the British colonial government the power to arrest and detains Indians without trial. Who was the British Viceroy of India at that time?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Lord Chelmsford.
  • Lord Chelmsford was the Viceroy of India (1916–1921) when the Rowlatt Act was passed.
  • The reforms of this era are known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919).
  • He was the Viceroy during the Non-Cooperation and Khilafat Movements.

questions.question: Who among the following was the second ruler of the Mauryan empire?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Bindusara.
  • Bindusara was the second Mauryan ruler, succeeding his father Chandragupta Maurya.
  • He is known as Amitraghata (Slayer of foes).
  • He was the father of Ashoka the Great.

questions.question: Who among the following had written the National anthem of Bangladesh 'Amar Sonar Bangla’?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Rabindranath Tagore.
  • 'Amar Sonar Bangla' (My Golden Bengal) was written by Rabindranath Tagore during the anti-partition movement in 1905.
  • It became the National Anthem of Bangladesh in 1971.
  • Tagore is the only person to have written the national anthems of two nations (India and Bangladesh).

questions.question: In which year was the Vernacular Press Act passed in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 1878.
  • The Vernacular Press Act was passed in 1878 by Lord Lytton.
  • It was nicknamed the 'Gagging Act' because it severely restricted the freedom of the non-English press.
  • It was later repealed by Lord Ripon in 1882.
